## Sampling Distributions for Non-Normal RVs

We learned that if a collection of independent random variables $X_1, X_2, \dots, X_n$ are normally distributed, then the sample mean is also normally distributed.

What if instead of being normally distributed, we have one of the following scenarios:

-   $X_i \overset{iid}{\sim} \text{Bernoulli}(p)$
-   $X_i \overset{iid}{\sim} \text{Binomial}(n, p)$
-   $X_i \overset{iid}{\sim} \text{Poisson}(\lambda)$
-   $X_i \overset{iid}{\sim} \text{Geometric}(p)$

Here $\overset{iid}{\sim}$ is a shortcut for saying the random variables are independent and identically distributed where identically distributed means they each have the same distribution with the same parameters.

## Central Limit Theorem

::: {.callout title="Theorem 19.1"}
If $X_1, X_2, \dots, X_n$ are independent and identically distributed random variables with mean $\text{E}[X_i] = \mu$ and variance $\text{Var}[X_i] = \sigma^2 < \infty$, then as $n \rightarrow \infty$:

$$
\sqrt{n}(\bar{X} - \mu) \overset{D}{\rightarrow} N(0, \sigma)
$$

For sufficiently large $n$ this means that:

$$
\bar{X} \overset{\cdot}{\sim} N\left(\mu, \frac{\sigma}{\sqrt{n}} \right)
$$
:::

Here $\overset{D}{\rightarrow}$ means converges in distribution and $\overset{\cdot}{\sim}$ means approximately distributed.

## Central Limit Theorem and Skew

The more skewed the underlying distribution, the larger a sample size you will need. For Bernoulli/Binomial distributions, the amount of skew is determined by $p$. If $p$ is very close to 0 or 1, the distribution will be very skewed.

For Bernoulli/Binomial distributions a good rule of thumb for the CLT to work is:

$$
np \geq 5 \text{ and } n(1-p) \geq 5
$$

For a Geometric distribution, the closer $p$ is to 0, the better. In contrast, for the Poisson distribution, a larger value of $\lambda$ will be better.

## Ex: Component Failures

::: {.callout title="Example 19.1"}
A manufacturer produces electronic components, and each component either passes or fails a quality control test. Suppose the probability that a randomly selected component passes the test is $p = 0.9$. A random sample of 50 components is selected, and the sample mean $\bar{X}$, which represents the proportion of passing components, is computed.

According to the Central Limit Theorem, what is the approximate sampling distribution of $\bar{X}$ (probability of a passing component)?
:::

. . .

According to the Central Limit Theorem we have the following:

$$
\begin{align}
\bar{X} & \overset{\cdot}{\sim} N\left(p, \sqrt{\frac{p(1-p)}{n}}\right) \\
& \overset{\cdot}{\sim} N\left(0.9, \sqrt{\frac{0.09}{50}}\right)
\end{align}
$$

## Ex: Defective Chips

::: {.callout title="Example 19.2"}
A quality control engineer is inspecting semiconductor chips produced in a factory. Each chip is independently classified as either defective or non-defective. Based on historical data, the probability that a randomly selected chip is defective is 0.1. You collect 50 ($n$) batches of 30 ($m$) chips each.

According to the Central Limit Theorem, what is the approximate sampling distribution of $\bar{X}$ (average number of defective chips)?
:::

. . .

According to the Central Limit Theorem we have:

$$
\begin{align}
\bar{X} & \overset{\cdot}{\sim} N\left(mp, \sqrt{\frac{m p(1-p)}{n}}\right) \\
& \overset{\cdot}{\sim} N\left(3, \sqrt{\frac{2.7}{50}}\right) 
\end{align}
$$

## Ex: Call Center

::: {.callout title="Example 19.3"}
A call center receives customer support calls at an average rate of 5 calls per hour. Assume that the number of calls received in an hour follows a Poisson distribution. You want to monitor the calls for 48 hours and record the number of calls in each hour.

According to the Central Limit Theorem, what is the approximate sampling distribution of $\bar{X}$ (average number of calls in an hour)?
:::

. . .

The Central Limit Theorem says the following for $\bar{X}$ in this case:

$$
\begin{align}
\bar{X} & \overset{\cdot}{\sim} N\left(\lambda, \sqrt{ \frac{\lambda}{n}}\right) \\
& \overset{\cdot}{\sim} N\left(5, \sqrt{ \frac{5}{48}}\right)
\end{align}
$$

## Ex: Component Inspection

::: {.callout title="Example 19.4"}
A manufacturer produces electronic components, and each component independently has a 0.1 probability of being defective. An inspector examines components one by one until they find the first defective component. They then repeat this process 50 times in all.

According to the Central Limit Theorem, what is the approximate sampling distribution of $\bar{X}$ (average number of working components before a defective one is found)?
:::

. . .

According to the Central Limit Theorem, we know that:

$$
\begin{align}
\bar{X} & \overset{\cdot}{\sim} N\left(\frac{1-p}{p}, \sqrt{\frac{1-p}{np^2}}\right) \\
& \overset{\cdot}{\sim} N\left(9, \sqrt{\frac{9}{5}}\right)
\end{align}
$$

## Ex: Component Failures

::: {.callout title="Example 19.5"}
A manufacturer produces electronic components, and each component either passes or fails a quality control test. Suppose the probability that a randomly selected component passes the test is $p = 0.9$. A random sample of 50 components is selected, and the sample mean $\bar{X}$, which represents the proportion of passing components, is computed.

What is the probability that the proportion of passing components is less than or equal to 0.88?
:::

. . .

$$
\begin{align}
\bar{X} \overset{\cdot}{\sim} N\left(0.9, \sqrt{\frac{0.09}{50}}\right)
\end{align}
$$

```{r, echo = TRUE}
p <- 0.9; mu_xbar <- p
n <- 50
sigma_xbar <- sqrt(p*(1-p)/n)

pnorm(0.88, mu_xbar, sigma_xbar) # Approximate Probability
pbinom(0.88*n, n, 0.9) # Exact Probability
```

## Ex: Call Center

::: {.callout title="Example 19.6"}
A call center receives customer support calls at an average rate of 5 calls per hour. Assume that the number of calls received in an hour follows a Poisson distribution. You want to monitor the calls for 48 hours and record the number of calls in each hour.

What is the probability that the average number of calls in an hour is less than or equal to 5?
:::

. . .

$$
\begin{align}
\bar{X} \overset{\cdot}{\sim} N\left(5, \sqrt{ \frac{5}{48}}\right)
\end{align}
$$

```{r, echo = TRUE}
lambda <- 5
mu_xbar <- lambda
sigma_xbar <- sqrt(lambda/48)

pnorm(5, mu_xbar, sigma_xbar) # Approximate Probability
ppois(48*5, 48*lambda) # Exact Probability
```

## Continuity Corrections

::: {.callout title="Theorem 19.2"}
Let $X_1, X_2, \dots, X_n$ be discrete random variables with mean $\text{E}[X_i] = \mu$ and standard deviation $\text{SD}[X_i] = \sigma$. Let $Y$ be a normal random variable with mean $\mu$ and standard deviation $\frac{\sigma}{\sqrt{n}}$ (the distribution used to approximate the sampling distribution of $\bar{X}$). This means $Y$ could be used to approximate the distribution of $\bar{X}$ and $nY$ could be used to approximate the distribution of $\sum_{i=1}^n X_i$. Then the following approximations hold:

$$
\begin{align}
P(\bar{X} \leq \bar{x}) &\simeq P\left(Y \leq \bar{x} + \frac{0.5}{n}\right) \\
P(\bar{X} < \bar{x}) &\simeq P\left(Y \leq \bar{x} - \frac{0.5}{n}\right) \\
P(\bar{X} \geq \bar{x}) &\simeq P\left(Y \geq \bar{x} - \frac{0.5}{n}\right) = 1- P\left(Y \leq \bar{x} - \frac{0.5}{n}\right)\\
P(\bar{X} > \bar{x}) &\simeq P\left(Y \geq \bar{x} + \frac{0.5}{n}\right) = 1- P\left(Y \leq \bar{x} + \frac{0.5}{n}\right) \\
\end{align}
$$
:::

## Continuity Corrections (Proof)

Below is a sketch of a proof for the first case:

$$
\begin{align}
P(\bar{X} \leq \bar{x}) &= P\left(\frac{1}{n} \sum_{i=1}^n X_i \leq \bar{x} \right) \\
&= P\left(\sum_{i=1}^n X_i \leq n\bar{x} \right) \\
&\simeq P\left(n Y \leq n\bar{x} + 0.5 \right) \\
&= P\left(Y \leq \bar{x} + \frac{0.5}{n} \right) \\
\end{align}
$$

## Ex: Component Failures

::: {.callout title="Example 19.5"}
A manufacturer produces electronic components, and each component either passes or fails a quality control test. Suppose the probability that a randomly selected component passes the test is $p = 0.9$. A random sample of 50 components is selected, and the sample mean $\bar{X}$, which represents the proportion of passing components, is computed.

What is the probability that the proportion of passing components is less than or equal to 0.88? Use CLT with continuity correction.
:::

. . .

$$
\begin{align}
\bar{X} \overset{\cdot}{\sim} N\left(0.9, \sqrt{\frac{0.09}{50}}\right)
\end{align}
$$

```{r, echo = TRUE}
p <- 0.9; mu_xbar <- p; n <- 50
sigma_xbar <- sqrt(p*(1-p)/n)

pnorm(0.88 + 0.5/n, mu_xbar, sigma_xbar) # Approximate Probability
pbinom(0.88*n, n, 0.9) # Exact Probability
```

## Ex: Call Center

::: {.callout title="Example 19.6"}
A call center receives customer support calls at an average rate of 5 calls per hour. Assume that the number of calls received in an hour follows a Poisson distribution. You want to monitor the calls for 48 hours and record the number of calls in each hour.

What is the probability that the average number of calls in an hour is less than or equal to 5? Use CLT with continuity correction.
:::

. . .

$$
\begin{align}
\bar{X} \overset{\cdot}{\sim} N\left(5, \sqrt{ \frac{5}{48}}\right)
\end{align}
$$

```{r, echo = TRUE}
lambda <- 5; n <- 48; mu_xbar <- lambda
sigma_xbar <- sqrt(lambda/n)

pnorm(5 + 0.5/n, mu_xbar, sigma_xbar) # Approximate Probability
ppois(48*5, 48*lambda) # Exact Probability
```

## Ex: Component Inspection

::: {.callout title="Example 19.7"}
A manufacturer produces electronic components, and each component independently has a 0.1 probability of being defective. An inspector examines components one by one until they find the first defective component. They then repeat this process 50 times in all.

What is the probability that the average number of working components tested before a defective one is found is more than 9.5? Use the CLT with a continuity correction.
:::

. . .

$$
\begin{align}
\bar{X} \overset{\cdot}{\sim} N\left(9, \sqrt{\frac{9}{5}}\right)
\end{align}
$$

. . .

```{r, echo = TRUE}
p <- 0.1
n <- 50
mu_xbar <- (1-p)/p
sigma_xbar <- sqrt((1-p)/(n*p^2))

1-pnorm(9.5 + 0.5/n, mu_xbar, sigma_xbar)
```

## Exact Bernoulli Probabilities

::: {.callout title="Theorem 19.1"}
If $X_1, X_2, \dots, X_n$ are independent and identically distributed Bernoulli random variables with success parameter $p$, then the following is true:

$$
P(\bar{X} \leq \bar{x}) = F_X(n \times \bar{x};n,p)
$$

where $F_X(x;n,p)$ is the CDF for a binomial distribution with parameters $n$ and $p$.
:::

. . .

$$
\begin{align}
P(\bar{X} \leq \bar{x}) &= P\left(\frac{1}{n} \sum_{i=1}^n X_i \leq \bar{x} \right) \\
&= P\left(\sum_{i=1}^n X_i \leq n \times \bar{x} \right) \\
&= F_X(n \times \bar{x};n,p) & \text{Since } \sum_{i=1}^n X_i \sim \text{Binomial}(n, p)
\end{align}
$$

## Exact Binomial Probabilities

::: {.callout title="Corollary 19.1"}
If $X_1, X_2, \dots, X_n$ are independent and identically distributed Binomial random variables with size parameter $m$ and success parameter $p$, then the following is true:

$$
P(\bar{X} \leq \bar{x}) = F_X(n \times \bar{x}; n \times m, p)
$$

where $F_X(n \times \bar{x}; n \times m, p)$ is the CDF for a Binomial distribution with size parameter $n \times m$ and success parameter $p$. The proof of this is very similar to the previous proof for the Bernoulli case.
:::

## Exact Poisson Probabilities

::: {.callout title="Corollary 19.2"}
If $X_1, X_2, \dots, X_n$ are independent and identically distributed Poisson random variables with rate parameter $\lambda$, then the following is true:

$$
P(\bar{X} \leq \bar{x}) = F_X(n \times \bar{x}; n \times \lambda)
$$

where $F_X(n \times \bar{x}; n \times \lambda)$ is the CDF for the Poisson distribution with rate parameter $n \times \lambda$.
:::

## Ex: Bus Passengers (1)

::: {.callout title="Example 19.8"}
A city bus stop experiences an average of 4 passengers arriving per minute. Assume the number of arrivals in a given minute follows a Poisson distribution. You are going to record the number of passengers each minute for an hour.

What is the probability that the average number of passengers in that hour greater than or equal to 4.5? Use the CLT with a continuity correction.
:::

. . .

$$
\begin{align}
\bar{X} \overset{\cdot}{\sim} N\left(4, \sqrt{\frac{4}{60}}\right)
\end{align}
$$

```{r, echo = TRUE}
lambda <- 4
n <- 60
mu_xbar <- lambda
sigma_xbar <- sqrt(lambda/n)

1-pnorm(4.5-0.5/n, mu_xbar, sigma_xbar)
```

## Ex: Bus Passengers (2)

::: {.callout title="Example 19.9"}
A city bus stop experiences an average of 4 passengers arriving per minute. Assume the number of arrivals in a given minute follows a Poisson distribution. You are going to record the number of passengers each minute for an hour.

What is the probability that the average number of passengers in that hour greater than or equal to 4.5? Compute the exact probability.
:::

. . .

```{r, echo = TRUE}
lambda <- 4
n <- 60

1-ppois(n*4.5-1, n*lambda)
```

## Ex: Website Purchases (1)

::: {.callout title="Example 19.10"}
A website tracks whether visitors make a purchase. Suppose that each visitor independently makes a purchase with probability 0.2. You plan to record the purchase decision for 40 customers. What is the probability that the proportion of purchases in your sample is less than 0.25? Use the CLT and a continuity correction.
:::

. . .

$$
\begin{align}
\bar{X} \overset{\cdot}{\sim} N\left(0.2, \sqrt{\frac{0.16}{40}}\right)
\end{align}
$$

```{r, echo = TRUE}
p <- 0.2
n <- 40
mu_xbar <- p
sigma_xbar <- sqrt(p*(1-p)/n)

pnorm(0.25-0.5/n, mu_xbar, sigma_xbar)
```

## Ex: Website Purchases (2)

::: {.callout title="Example 19.11"}
A website tracks whether visitors make a purchase. Suppose that each visitor independently makes a purchase with probability 0.2. You plan to record the purchase decision for 40 customers. What is the probability that the proportion of purchases in your sample is less than 0.25? Compute the exact probability.
:::

. . .

```{r, echo = TRUE}
p <- 0.2
n <- 40

pbinom(n*0.25-1, n, p)
```

## Ex: Website Purchases (3)

::: {.callout title="Example 19.12"}
A website tracks whether visitors make a purchase. Suppose that each visitor independently makes a purchase with probability 0.2. You plan to look at 50 groups of 30 visitors each and count the number of purchases made for each group.

What is the probability that the average number of purchases in a group is less than or equal to 5.6? Use the CLT and a continuity correction.
:::

. . .

$$
\begin{align}
\bar{X} \overset{\cdot}{\sim} N\left(6, \sqrt{\frac{4.8}{50}}\right)
\end{align}
$$

```{r, echo = TRUE}
p <- 0.2
n <- 50
m <- 30
mu_xbar <- m*p
sigma_xbar <- sqrt(m*p*(1-p)/n)

pnorm(5.6+0.5/n, mu_xbar, sigma_xbar)
```

## Ex: Website Purchases (4)

::: {.callout title="Example 19.13"}
A website tracks whether visitors make a purchase. Suppose that each visitor independently makes a purchase with probability 0.2. You plan to look at 50 groups of 30 visitors each and count the number of purchases made for each group.

What is the probability that the average number of purchases in a group is less than or equal to 5.6? Compute the exact probability.
:::

. . .

```{r, echo = TRUE}
p <- 0.2
n <- 50
m <- 30

pbinom(n*5.6, n*m, p)
```
